purpose: Preserve distinct published economic, regulatory, insurability and port-readiness claims as separate evidence-bounded benchmark anchors. No result is generalized beyond its stated scope.

anchors.title: Nuclear Reactors for Merchant Shipping: A Total Cost of Ownership Assessment of a Low-Carbon Pathway
public_summary_findings: Without the IMO Net-Zero Framework, no nuclear-powered vessel in the study is cheaper than conventional vessels, even at the lowest assumed reactor costs.
Under the IMO Net-Zero Framework, nuclear propulsion could become the least-cost option from 2040 if reactor costs fall significantly.
The reactor-cost reductions required for that result have not yet been demonstrated.
Insurance, liability and regulation remain important barriers.
missing_for_full_reproduction: Vessel classes, routes, operating profiles and comparator definitions
Fuel-cycle, staffing, maintenance and outage assumptions
Insurance, liability, port access and regulatory treatment
IMO Net-Zero Framework policy and carbon-cost assumptions
inference_limits: Does not prove nuclear shipping is uneconomic in every route, time period or policy regime.
Does not establish that nuclear becomes least-cost in 2040; that result is explicitly conditional.
Does not provide a license, class approval, insurance quote or operating demonstration.
The PDF states document publication date 27 October 2026; the UCL public page release date is 5 November 2026. Preserve both timestamps.
The low-CAPEX 2040 outcome is conditional on NOAK/series-production costs and policy assumptions, not a demonstrated reactor price or deployment forecast.

The UCL high-speed result is driven by explicit cube-law power scaling and linear CAPEX-per-kWe scaling; alternative power or cost exponents must be separate sensitivity cases, not silently substituted.
The study is a per-vessel TCO comparison and does not use fleet adoption outputs.

publication_metadata.note: The document's internal publication details and the public UCL page's release date differ; preserve both.

published_model_details.model_scope: Per-vessel propulsion cost comparison; fleet adoption outcomes of the inherited model are not used.

reactor_capex_usd_per_kwe.scaling_assumption: Reactor CAPEX applied linearly per installed kWe, including auxiliary capacity.

policy_and_fuel_scenarios: IMO Net-Zero Framework with low biofuel price
IMO Net-Zero Framework with high biofuel price
No IMO Net-Zero Framework and low biofuel price

result_summary.no_policy: No nuclear case is cheaper than the conventional vessel; low-CAPEX 14.85-knot nuclear is closest.
result_summary.nzf_low_biofuel: Low-CAPEX nuclear at 14.85 knots is the cheapest option from its model introduction in 2040; high-CAPEX nuclear remains more expensive than the conventional and ammonia benchmarks.
result_summary.nzf_high_biofuel: Low-CAPEX nuclear at 14.85 knots is cheapest from 2040. The low-CAPEX 25-knot case is cheaper than conventional throughout and cheaper than ammonia in the first years after introduction, but higher TCO than the 14.85-knot nuclear case.
result_summary.speed_comparison: At 25 knots, the nuclear vessel's TCO per tonne-nautical-mile is higher than the same CAPEX case at 14.85 knots.

policy_modeling_notes.interpretation: The report says its reward mechanism is included for e-fuels such as e-ammonia but not nuclear SMR; it notes that reactors could in principle be eligible if well-to-wake zero-GHG emissions are delivered. Keep eligibility as a separate policy sensitivity rather than silently crediting nuclear.
policy_modeling_notes.low_speed_low_capex_case: Least-cost from NOAK nuclear introduction in 2040 under NZF scenarios.
policy_modeling_notes.no_policy_case: No GFI targets or surplus-unit revenue; no nuclear case is cheaper than the conventional vessel.

power_speed_scaling.interpretation: Published model inputs imply installed-power scaling of about 3.20x for about 1.32x annual distance. Ratios are arithmetic derived from the published inputs, not additional measured data.

known_cost_limitations: Decommissioning is included only as a rough estimate.
UCL states these gaps are likely to understate nuclear shipping costs.

anchors.title: Power Shift: Nuclear Power Pathways for Future Containership Fleets
public_summary_findings: The study estimates up to 38% greater annual cargo capacity for the scenario relative to its conventional reference.
Eliminating conventional fuel tanks is estimated to free up to 5% additional container space.
missing_for_full_reproduction: Exact ship power and propulsion assumptions
Route, speed, weather, port dwell and voyage schedule
Nuclear CAPEX, financing and lifecycle-cost assumptions
Comparator vessel and lifecycle emissions assumptions
inference_limits: Modeled maximum gains are not achieved fleet performance.
The case cannot be generalized to all containership sizes, speeds or routes.
The result must not be treated as directly inconsistent with UCL until system boundaries and assumptions are reconciled.
LR reports a scenario-specific modeled 15,000 TEU / 25-knot case; its public summary is insufficient to independently reconstruct all annual TCO inputs.
LR's total-system-cost threshold in USD/kW is not directly interchangeable with UCL's reactor CAPEX in USD/kWe.
The annual cargo-capacity uplift, voyage count and freed container-space figures are modeled claims, not observed fleet performance.

public_summary_details.public_evidence_boundary: Public case-study summary; detailed ship power, CAPEX, financing and full cost model inputs are not disclosed in the summary.
public_summary_details.relative_speed_comparison_basis: The summary describes the 25-knot nuclear case as 39% faster than conventional vessels; it does not state the exact conventional reference speed in that public summary.
public_summary_details.public_data_sufficiency: The public summary is enough to freeze headline service/cost-threshold claims, but not enough to reconstruct full installed power, financing, detailed cost ledger, route assumptions or uncertainty distributions.

anchors.title: The economics of nuclear propulsion for containerships
public_summary_findings: The study uses levelized cost of transport to compare nuclear propulsion with conventional and alternative-fuel systems.
The abstract reports potential competitiveness in specific scenarios involving high cruising speeds and favorable nuclear-reactor CAPEX.
It identifies learning from building and operating containerships as a potential contributor to scale economics.
missing_for_full_reproduction: Detailed model assumptions and sensitivity ranges
Exact route, speed and utilization comparison
Reactor CAPEX, financing, fuel-cycle, port and insurance assumptions
inference_limits: A positive scenario is not a fleet-wide commercial result.
Do not assume its model is numerically comparable with UCL or LR without reconstructing all boundaries.

anchors.title: Nuclear Propulsion
public_summary_findings: Conventional marine insurance excludes nuclear risks.
Existing maritime liability conventions and the IMO framework were not designed for nuclear-powered merchant ships.
Repair, decommissioning and port-access concerns remain.
inference_limits: This is an industry policy position; project-specific legal and insurance structures still require direct analysis.
Do not infer that a future insurance or liability arrangement is impossible.

anchors.title: Nuclear shipping's second act
public_summary_findings: Port exclusion in key markets could undermine commercial viability.
Insurers need clarity on realistic loss scenarios and responsibility allocation among shipowner, reactor operator, technology provider and government.
Insurance and reinsurer engagement should begin during design and contracting, not after construction.
inference_limits: The publication identifies questions and barriers; it does not provide an insurer quote or a universal insurability determination.

anchors.title: Advanced Nuclear Technology Use Within Port Environments
public_summary_findings: Ports should prepare before procurement through stakeholder mapping, demand and grid assessment, regulator engagement, workforce capability and evidence-led community communication.
Applications include nuclear ship calls, floating power units and land-based SMRs.
The report describes a staged readiness pathway from nuclear-aware through nuclear-ready and nuclear-enabled to a nuclear energy hub.
Nuclear will not be appropriate for every port.
inference_limits: Readiness labels are not licensing or deployment approval.
No port is declared suitable by this registry.

anchors.title: IMO Nuclear Code and SOLAS Chapter VIII revision work
public_summary_findings: The workplan targets future revision milestones through 2030.
inference_limits: Planned milestones are not adopted requirements in force.
The workplan does not grant vessel or port authorization.

anchors.title: NEA Small Modular Reactor Digital Dashboard — Fourth Edition
public_summary_findings: The dashboard tracks 156 SMR and micro-modular reactor projects, with 95 included in the assessed dashboard.
Readiness dimensions include licensing, siting, financing, supply chain, engagement and fuel.
inference_limits: Project counts are not the same as operating units or demonstrated cost competitiveness.
A technology's readiness must be assessed per project and jurisdiction.

comparison_rules: Never average study conclusions or merge numerical results before matching vessel class, route, service level, speed, utilization, CAPEX, financing, fuel, maintenance, insurance, port access, policy and lifecycle boundaries.
Preserve each published claim as a separate evidence object with its date, scope, maturity and missing assumptions.
Do not hard-code published conclusions into the economic calculator.
A scenario may be technically possible but commercially infeasible because mandatory port, insurance, liability, emergency, fuel-cycle or licensing gates fail.
Use UNKNOWN where evidence is missing; do not turn missing data into a favorable assumption.
Separate model outputs, industry estimates, regulator decisions, insurer decisions and observed vessel/plant performance.

Reconcile the UCL and LR speed results by first freezing each study's speed-to-installed-power law, reactor CAPEX scaling, auxiliary load, annual voyage schedule, port dwell and transport-work denominator.
Do not equate UCL reactor CAPEX in USD/kWe with LR total-system cost thresholds in USD/kW.
Reproduce the UCL no-policy case as a mandatory negative control before testing any policy-supported or high-throughput case.

The UCL high-speed 25-knot case has over three times installed electrical power and higher TCO per tonne-nautical-mile than its 14.85-knot nuclear counterpart; do not claim speed inherently improves nuclear economics.
Separate annual cargo-capacity uplift, freed cargo volume, fuel cost savings, carbon-policy credits and delivered transport work to prevent double counting.
prohibited_inferences: Do not claim that commercial nuclear shipping is already generally cost competitive.
Do not claim the UCL conditional 2040 result is guaranteed.
Do not claim the LR 38% annual cargo capacity estimate is realized or universally applicable.
Do not claim the academic scenario result demonstrates a commercial fleet.
Do not equate the number of SMR projects with qualified, financeable or operating designs.
